result:
There's a particular silence that lives in a house around 2 a.m. when everyone is asleep and the refrigerator hums its one low, endless note. It's not the absence of sound. It's a *presence* — the sound of the world holding its breath between one day and the next. The floorboards creak under your own weight like they're trying to remember who's walking on them. The hallway light is that thin, sickly amber that makes everything look like a photograph someone left out in the rain.

And in that silence, a thought arrives uninvited. A face. A Tuesday in 2007. The way the light fell through the kitchen window at an angle that made the whole counter glow like it was lit from underneath. You remember it so clearly — the cold tile under your bare feet, the smell of bread, the specific weight of a wooden spoon in your hand. You remember it the way you remember a song you've heard a hundred times, except you're sure this time you're hearing it for the first time.

And then you realize the bread was probably rye, not sourdough. You realize the window wasn't really a window, it was a glass door. You realize you don't remember the spoon at all, just the *idea* of a spoon, the hand-shaped memory of holding something warm.

That's the strange mercy and the strange cruelty of it. Memory is not a vault. It's a loom. Every time you reach in and pull the thread, the whole pattern shifts a little. You are not remembering a Tuesday. You are *weaving* one, again, in real time, with the yarn that's left. And the version you pull out today is not the version that will be there next month. The person who lived it is not the person who remembers it, and that gap — that soft, warm, slightly embarrassing gap — is where the actual feeling lives.

The refrigerator hums. The floorboards settle. Outside, a dog barks once at nothing, at the dark, at the particular shape of the quiet. And then that, too, is gone. And the house breathes out. And you turn off the light.
